source.title: How do language models learn facts? Dynamics, curricula and hallucinations
source.authors: Nicolas Zucchet; Jörg Bornschein; Stephanie Chan; A. Lampinen; Razvan Pascanu; Soham De

record.file_problem: Full paper and appendix are present; no apparent garbling or cutoff.
record.tranche_reason: Tests delayed learning dynamics and developing recall circuits in a new setting: synthetic factual biographies rather than the algorithmic datasets in the claim.
record.gate_note: The study reports delayed acquisition on synthetic factual recall data, but does not test modular arithmetic or another algorithmic dataset, nor report training accuracy saturating before held-out accuracy rises. It measures performance on new biography formulations for individuals seen during training. Its fine-tuning and hallucination findings do not measure the claim versions. Several plotted outcomes are described qualitatively but lack extractable numerical values.
record.test_reason: The study shows a loss plateau followed by knowledge acquisition on synthetic biographies. Grokking means a gap between training and held-out performance, and this study shows none. Training loss (Figure A left) plateaus alongside held-out-template loss, so there is no saturated training fit followed by delayed generalization. That makes it abrupt-learning or plateau dynamics, a related but different construct. Grokking appears only in a speculative Discussion remark (shortcut abandoned under regularization), which the authors do not test.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors find three phases (statistics, plateau, knowledge emergence), with recall attention circuits forming during the plateau. Imbalanced distributions shorten the plateau but hurt final acquisition, and warm-up scheduling helps. Hallucinations emerge with knowledge, and fine-tuning on new individuals rapidly corrupts feed-forward memories. Their link to grokking is only a speculative remark in the Discussion, not a tested conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: Uses synthetic biographies and attribute recall with a Transformer trained using AdamW, rather than an algorithmic dataset such as modular arithmetic. Evaluates held-out biography templates for familiar individuals.
record.method_sensitivity: Plateau length and final retrieval performance vary with population size and individual sampling distribution. Attention patterns from early checkpoints can be worse than pre-learning patterns, while post-plateau patterns remove the plateau.

fits_no_version.finding: In a synthetic factual-recall task, training and held-out loss both sit at the no-knowledge baseline for a plateau. During the plateau, attention-based recall circuits form, shown by attention patching and rising name-token attention. Knowledge then emerges.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss plateaus in factual-recall training coincide with the formation of attention extraction circuits, which precede the drop in loss.

fits_no_version.finding: Plateau length scales nearly linearly with the number of individuals (exponent 0.81, R²=0.998). Moderate imbalance in how often individuals are sampled (α 0.6–0.8) shortens it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In associative-recall training, plateau duration is set by how often each individual is seen, so data imbalance or a warm-up schedule shortens it.

record.problems: The main task is synthetic factual recall, not an algorithmic dataset; models are relatively small. The paper reports 5 seeds for Figure 2 but a single seed for most other experiments. Several attention-patching values are presented only in figures, without numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Fine-tuning, hallucination, and replay outcomes were not included because they do not measure the delayed-generalization or circuit-development behaviors in the tested versions. Distribution-scheduling results on final performance were also omitted where they did not separately report a result on plateau duration or the specified circuit measures.

untested.parts: No algorithmic dataset, no train-saturation-then-test-jump, no training-set-size sweep of a generalization delay.
No generalizing-vs-memorizing circuit analysis, no removal of memorization, no progress measure for a grokking jump.
No grokking-like train–test delay on non-algorithmic data. No initialization-scale or weight-norm switching, and no lazy-to-rich transition.
No realistic large-model pretraining or fine-tuning data.
Weight decay appears only as a robustness ablation (Figure C). No critical dataset size, no ungrokking.
No comparison of algorithms learned across runs.

missing.what: The training loss curve plateaus in parallel with held-out-template attribute loss, showing no train–test gap. This is key to ruling out grokking.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked rows to V2 and V3 by analogy with grokking. The plateau here occurs in training loss too, so it is not delayed generalization. All rows are relinked to 'none', no verdicts are given, and the findings are recorded under fits_no_version. A single seed is used outside Figure 2.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not use a small algorithmic dataset or report training accuracy saturating before test accuracy rises. Its synthetic factual-recall task is not the algorithmic setting specified by this version.

Tests attention-based recall circuit development and attention patching, but not Fourier algorithms, removal of memorizing components, or whether the measured progress anticipates a grokking jump on an algorithmic task.

Tests synthetic biography data and changes to the individual sampling distribution. Does not test image, molecule, or realistic natural-text corpora, initialization scale, or a lazy-to-rich transition controlled by weight norm.
No realistic large-model pretraining or fine-tuning.
Does not test an efficiency account, critical dataset size, or ungrokking. Weight-decay ablations are reported as robustness checks, not as tests of this account.
Does not identify or compare algorithms learned across runs.
Does not test adaptive-optimizer instability or floating-point/softmax artifacts as explanations for grokking.

rows.subject: 8-layer decoder-only Transformer (44M non-embedding parameters)
rows.operation_detail: Train on synthetic biographies; track attribute accuracy on unseen biography formulations for seen individuals.
rows.baseline: Near-zero knowledge accuracy at the no-knowledge baseline
rows.value: Accuracy progressively leaves the near-zero regime during the knowledge-acquisition phase after a performance plateau.
rows.uncertainty: Results averaged over 5 seeds (± std); numerical error-bar values not stated in the text.
rows.note: The authors describe a plateau followed by progressive acquisition, not a sudden jump to near-perfect accuracy. No training-accuracy curve is reported.
rows.check: Measures a loss plateau shared by training and held-out templates, not delayed generalization after training saturation. It does not bear on V3's grokking-like delay.

rows.subject: 8-layer decoder-only Transformer (44M non-embedding parameters)
rows.operation_detail: Vary the number of individuals and measure plateau end.
rows.value: Plateau end follows y = 0.43 x^0.81; R² = 0.998. The text says plateau duration grows almost linearly with the number of individuals.
rows.uncertainty: ± std shown in Figure 2; numerical values not stated.
rows.note: The population-size sweep measures the duration of the plateau, but population size is not the same manipulation as shrinking an algorithmic training set.
rows.check: The plateau length grows with population size (y = 0.43x^0.81). This is a training plateau, not a train–test generalization delay, and more individuals is not the same as a smaller training set.

rows.subject: 8-layer decoder-only Transformer (44M non-embedding parameters)
rows.operation_detail: Vary the inverse-power-law exponent α of the individual sampling distribution and measure plateau duration.

conditions.value: inverse power law; α varied from 0 (uniform) to 1 (Zipf)

rows.measure: Steps needed to escape the plateau
rows.value: Increasing α reduces plateau length; the reported optimum for minimizing plateau length lies between 0.6 and 0.8, irrespective of population size. Excessive increases are detrimental, likely due to overfitting.
rows.note: The plotted values are not numerically tabulated in the text.
rows.check: Sampling imbalance (α) shortens the shared plateau. This is not a grokking delay measure.

rows.subject: 8-layer decoder-only Transformer (44M non-embedding parameters)
rows.operation_detail: Track attention to name tokens when predicting the first attribute-value token.

conditions.value: initial phase through plateau and later training

rows.baseline: Attention to name tokens is significantly lower in the initial phase.
rows.value: Attention to name tokens increases throughout the plateau.
rows.note: This is a progress measure for attention patterns; it is not a measure of removal of memorizing components.
rows.check: Name-token attention rises during the plateau. This is a continuous measure preceding a training-loss drop, not a generalization jump after memorization, and there is no Fourier circuit or memorization-removal analysis.

reader_labels.condition: Reference attention patterns at 500 and 1k steps
reader_labels.reason: These early learned patterns are reported to be worse for learning than pre-learning patterns, so progress is not uniformly beneficial from the start (r5, r6).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The model exhibits a delayed plateau followed by increasing held-out-template accuracy in this non-algorithmic synthetic language task (r1, r2).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Plateau duration depends on the data distribution: increasing imbalance shortens it only up to an extent, with excessive imbalance reported as detrimental (r3).
